# The Rosebush Fence

Maya had taken the shortcut home a hundred times.

The old wooden fence behind the Kellerman property sat between her and the back of her neighborhood, and at fourteen, she had developed the casual confidence of someone who had cleared it dozens of times without incident. Backpack over one shoulder, mind already drifting toward the homework she was dreading, she grabbed the top rail and swung her legs over.

She heard it before she felt it.

A sharp, catastrophic *rip*.

The hem of her yellow sundress — the new one her mother had bought specifically for the class photos taken that morning — had caught on a protruding nail at the top of the fence post. The momentum of her jump did the rest. By the time her sneakers hit the grass on the other side, the dress had been torn completely away, left hanging on the fence like a defeated flag while Maya stood in nothing but her white sneakers and the plain underwear she had chosen that morning without any thought whatsoever to the possibility of public display.

For one full second, she stood completely still.

Then the reality of her situation arrived like cold water.

She spun and grabbed for the dress. It was shredded beyond any hope of wearing — the fabric had torn along the entire bodice seam, leaving roughly half of it still impaled on the nail and the other half a useless strip of yellow cotton. She held both pieces up and immediately understood that no combination of them would help her.

She was standing behind a property that was not hers, in a semi-open area visible from the road that ran parallel to the neighborhood.

She made a sound that was not quite a word.

Her backpack. She ripped it open with shaking hands and dug through it with the desperate energy of someone defusing something. A binder. A pencil case. A library book. A crumpled permission slip. Her lunch bag, which was soft-sided and approximately the size of a hardcover novel and therefore useless. There was a gym shirt somewhere in there — she remembered leaving it — but her hands found only a rolled-up pair of socks.

She pressed the lunch bag against herself anyway, knowing it was absurd, doing it regardless.

Her face was burning. She could feel heat climbing from her chest up through her neck and into her ears with such intensity that it was almost painful. Her eyes had gone glassy, not quite crying but on the close side of it, the way they did when embarrassment reached a certain unbearable threshold.

She crouched behind her backpack as though that helped.

*Think,* she told herself. *Think, think, think.*

She could call her mother. The thought lasted about two seconds before she understood that her mother would answer, hear the situation, and Maya would be able to hear the precise quality of silence that preceded the question *How exactly did this happen?* along with the information that today, of all days, was the day the photos were going to be framed.

She could run. She actually measured the distance in her head — maybe sixty yards of open ground between her and the back gate of her own yard. Sixty yards of afternoon light, with the road visible on her left.

She was still crouching, the torn yellow fabric balled in one fist, when she heard the footsteps on the gravel path that ran along the fence.

She dropped lower and felt her whole body go rigid.

The footsteps belonged to Mr. Alderton, who lived three houses down and who she knew vaguely as the man who grew tomatoes in stacked planters and waved at cars. He was probably sixty, white-haired, wearing a fleece jacket despite the mild weather, carrying what appeared to be a small bag of gardening supplies.

He stopped.

The pause lasted long enough to understand he had seen her.

Maya had faced difficult social situations before. She had mispronounced a word in front of her entire English class. She had called her teacher *Mom* in fifth grade. She had fallen off a chair during a presentation. Each of those moments had seemed, at the time, like the concentrated essence of mortification.

This was something else entirely.

She couldn't speak. She was holding a lunch bag and a ruined dress and crouching behind a backpack in Mr. Alderton's neighbor's backyard, and she genuinely considered whether it was possible to simply cease to exist through willpower alone.

Mr. Alderton turned around immediately. He turned around so quickly and completely that it was clearly intentional, staring with great interest at the fence on the opposite side of the path.

"I'm going to set something down here," he said, to the fence, in the same conversational tone he might use to discuss tomato yields. "On this post here. And then I'm going to go back and check on my planters, which need a good deal of attention, over that way."

She heard the rustle of the fleece jacket. Heard it come off. Heard it land on the post.

"No hurry," he said, already walking away. "Take your time."

His footsteps moved steadily away from her, unhurried, and then turned and disappeared.

Maya stayed crouched for a moment longer. Then she crossed the few feet to the post in a half-run and pulled the jacket around herself with hands that were not entirely steady. It fell to mid-thigh, green fleece, smelling like cedar and fresh dirt. She zipped it to the chin.

She stood there for a moment, alone behind the fence.

The burning in her face was not going away. It occurred to her that it might simply live there permanently now, a reminder, the way a scar does. She pressed the back of her wrist against her cheek and exhaled slowly.

She walked the rest of the way home.

She left the ruined dress in the outside recycling bin rather than explain it to anyone. She went upstairs, changed, came down, and ate dinner and said very little.

A week later she walked to Mr. Alderton's door with the jacket freshly washed and folded, and when he opened it she held it out and looked somewhere around his left ear and said, *Thank you for this,* very quickly.

"Found it on a post," he said simply, and took it back, and that was the whole of it.

She walked home faster than necessary.

The burning came back, brief and total, and then — finally — faded.
